the PS rule is simple: *document what's there*. The previous integrator left no notes.

You have read-write CLI on **FGT-SR**. Collect the facts the customer's IT lead asked for and answer below.

parts.title: First contact with a FortiGate you've never seen
tasks: Find the hostname, the serial number and the firmware version.
Find which interface and gateway the default route uses.
Find which firewall policy publishes the appointment portal (citas.clinicasanrafael.co).

ran.fail: Start with `get system status`: it's the first command on any new FortiGate.

ran.cmd: get router info routing-table|get router info rout

answer.hint: It's in the output of `get system status`, the Serial-Number line.
answer.why: Serial numbers go in every PS report and every TAC case.

checks.text: Default route: which interface and gateway? (e.g. port1 192.0.2.1)

answer.hint: Look for the S* line in the routing table.

checks.text: Which policy ID publishes the portal?

answer.hint: `show firewall policy`, look for the policy whose destination is a VIP.
answer.why: Policy 2 (Citas-Publish) allows HTTPS from wan1 to the VIP VIP-CITAS-443.

hints: Three read-only commands answer everything: one for the system, one for routing, one for policies.
`get system status`, `get router info routing-table all`, `show firewall policy`.

solution.FGT-SR:
get system status
get router info routing-table all
show firewall policy

parts.explain:
A PS consultant's first hour on an unknown box is read-only. `get system status` gives model, firmware,
serial, HA mode and VDOM mode; the routing table tells you how traffic leaves; `show firewall policy`
shows what's allowed. Note what you find before you touch anything: it's your baseline and your rollback.

parts.title: show, get and full-configuration
tasks: Find the default admin idle timeout (it isn't in `show system global`, because it's a default).
Rename the FortiGate to FGT-SR-SMR01 (site SR, city code SMR, unit 01).
Set the admin idle timeout to 15 minutes.
Give the dmz interface the alias "DMZ-Portal".

checks.text: What is the default admintimeout, in minutes?

answer.hint: `show full-configuration system global`, then find admintimeout. Or `get system global`.
answer.why: Defaults never appear in plain `show`; that's why reading a config needs full-configuration.

hints: `show` hides defaults. Try `show full-configuration system global` or `get system global`.
`config system global`, then `set hostname ...` and `set admintimeout ...`, then `end`.
Aliases live on the interface: `config system interface`, `edit dmz`, `set alias DMZ-Portal`.

solution.FGT-SR:
show full-configuration system global
config system global
set hostname FGT-SR-SMR01
set admintimeout 15
end
config system interface
edit dmz
set alias DMZ-Portal
next
end

parts.explain:
Changes in an `edit` take effect at `next` or `end`; `abort` throws them away. When you document a
customer's config, use `show` to see their intent and `show full-configuration` when a default matters.
The prompt changes with the hostname immediately: that's how you know `end` committed it.

parts.title: Back up before you touch anything
tasks: Back up the configuration to TFTP 10.10.10.50 before any change (file name of your choice).
Rename WEB-CITAS to SRV-CITAS-WEB and check that policy 3 still works.
Delete OLD-PRINTER.
Try to delete LAN-Staff, read the error, and answer why it failed.

checks.text: Configuration backed up before the first change
SRV-CITAS-WEB exists and policy 3 uses it
Staff can still reach the portal over HTTPS

answer.hint: Read the error: 'The entry is used by other ... entries'.
answer.why: FortiOS won't delete an object a policy references. Rename updates references for you; delete doesn't.

hints: The backup command starts with `execute backup config tftp`, then a file name, then the server IP.
`config firewall address`, then `rename WEB-CITAS to SRV-CITAS-WEB`, then `delete OLD-PRINTER`.

solution.FGT-SR:
execute backup config tftp fgt-sr-before-cleanup.conf 10.10.10.50
config firewall address
rename WEB-CITAS to SRV-CITAS-WEB
delete OLD-PRINTER
delete LAN-Staff
end

parts.explain:
`rename` keeps every reference pointing at the object; delete-and-recreate would break the policies that use it.
FortiOS refuses to delete an object in use ("The entry is used by other N entries"); you'd first remove it from
each policy. And the backup comes first: it's your rollback if the window goes wrong.

parts.title: Read the routing table and the session table
tasks: From RECEPCION, browse to www.fortinet.com (curl https://www.fortinet.com) so a session exists.
On FGT-SR, filter the session list to RECEPCION's IP and read the session.
Find which interface traffic to 172.16.40.15 would use.

ran.fail: Run curl https://www.fortinet.com on RECEPCION first.
Filter first: `diagnose sys session filter src <ip>`, then `diagnose sys session list`.

checks.text: Which policy ID handled RECEPCION's web session?

answer.hint: Look for policy_id= in the session.
answer.why: policy_id=1 (Staff-Internet).

checks.text: Which source IP did the session leave with (after SNAT)?

answer.hint: The act=snat line shows the translated address in brackets.
answer.why: SNAT to wan1's IP, 203.0.113.2.

checks.text: Which interface would traffic to 172.16.40.15 leave through?

answer.hint: `get router info routing-table details 172.16.40.15`.
answer.why: The static route 172.16.40.0/24 via 10.10.10.254 points out internal.

hints: Session list is long on a real box. Always filter: `diagnose sys session filter clear`, then `diagnose sys session filter src <RECEPCION IP>`.
RECEPCION's IP comes from DHCP: run ipconfig there.

solution.FGT-SR:
diagnose sys session filter clear
diagnose sys session filter src 10.10.10.100
diagnose sys session list
get router info routing-table details 172.16.40.15

parts.explain:
The session table is the truth about traffic the FortiGate has already accepted: interfaces, gateway,
NAT and the policy ID. In production it holds thousands of entries, so filter first. `routing-table details <ip>`
answers "where would this go" without sending a packet.

labs.title: Clínica San Rafael: day-one deployment
labs.customer: Clínica San Rafael (40 staff, Santa Marta)
labs.brief:
**SOW 2026-118 · FortiGate-60F deployment.** The clinic replaces a consumer router with a FortiGate-60F.

**In scope:** WAN on Claro (203.0.113.2/28, gateway 203.0.113.1), staff LAN 10.10.10.0/24 with DHCP,
a DMZ for the appointment portal (WEB-CITAS, 192.168.50.10), Internet for staff, publishing the portal
over HTTPS only, and admin hardening.
**Out of scope:** Wi-Fi, VPN, security profiles (phase 2).
**Change window:** tonight 20:00–23:00. **Acceptance:** the checks of each part.

The project has five parts. Each one unlocks when the previous one passes, like the milestones of a real SOW.

topology.title: Clínica San Rafael · Santa Marta

parts.title: Interfaces and management access
parts.brief: Address the three interfaces. Management (HTTPS, SSH) only from the staff LAN; the WAN answers ping and nothing else.
tasks: wan1: 203.0.113.2/28, allow ping only, alias Claro.
internal: 10.10.10.1/24, allow ping, HTTPS and SSH, alias LAN-Staff.
dmz: 192.168.50.1/24, allow ping only.

checks.text: No HTTPS, HTTP, SSH or Telnet admin on wan1
The portal server pings its gateway 192.168.50.1
The DMZ can't open the GUI

hints: Everything here is under `config system interface`, one `edit` per port.
allowaccess replaces the whole list: `set allowaccess ping https ssh`.
`edit wan1` / `set ip 203.0.113.2/28` / `set allowaccess ping` / `set alias Claro` / `next`.

solution.FGT-SR:
config system interface
edit wan1
set ip 203.0.113.2/28
set allowaccess ping
set alias Claro
next
edit internal
set ip 10.10.10.1/24
set allowaccess ping https ssh
set alias LAN-Staff
next
edit dmz
set ip 192.168.50.1/24
set allowaccess ping
next
end

parts.explain:
allowaccess controls which management services an interface answers. Exposing HTTPS or SSH on a WAN is the most
common finding in FortiGate health checks; it's also the first thing attackers scan for.

parts.title: DHCP and DNS for staff
parts.brief:
Staff PCs use DHCP. Leases from 10.10.10.100 to 10.10.10.199, gateway 10.10.10.1. The FortiGate uses Google and
Cloudflare as DNS, and hands the same servers to the PCs.
tasks: System DNS: primary 8.8.8.8, secondary 1.1.1.1.
DHCP server on internal: range 10.10.10.100-10.10.10.199, gateway 10.10.10.1, mask 255.255.255.0, DNS = the system DNS.
Renew the lease on RECEPCION (ipconfig /renew) and check it.

checks.text: RECEPCION gets an address in 10.10.10.100-199 with gateway 10.10.10.1

hints: DNS: `config system dns` / `set primary ...` / `set secondary ...` / `end`.
The range is a table inside the DHCP server: `config ip-range` / `edit 1` / `set start-ip ...` / `set end-ip ...` / `next` / `end`.
`set dns-service default` hands out the FortiGate's own system DNS servers.

solution.FGT-SR:
config system dns
set primary 8.8.8.8
set secondary 1.1.1.1
end
config system dhcp server
edit 1
set interface internal
set default-gateway 10.10.10.1
set netmask 255.255.255.0
set dns-service default
config ip-range
edit 1
set start-ip 10.10.10.100
set end-ip 10.10.10.199
next
end
next
end

parts.explain:
dns-service has three modes: default (system DNS), specify (dns-server1/2) and local (the FortiGate itself as a DNS
server). Most "Internet doesn't work" tickets on day one are a DHCP lease without a DNS server.

parts.title: Internet for staff
parts.brief: Staff browse the Internet through Claro. Use an address object for the LAN and source NAT to wan1's IP.
tasks: Default route to 203.0.113.1 through wan1.
Address object LAN-Staff = 10.10.10.0/24.
Policy internal → wan1 for LAN-Staff, NAT enabled, named Staff-Internet.

checks.text: The policy uses the LAN-Staff object, not 'all'

hints: Without a route the FortiGate drops the packet before any policy: check `get router info routing-table all`.
`config router static` / `edit 0` / `set gateway 203.0.113.1` / `set device wan1` / `next` / `end`.
Private 10.x addresses can't come back from the Internet: the policy needs `set nat enable`.

solution.FGT-SR:
config router static
edit 0
set gateway 203.0.113.1
set device wan1
next
end
config firewall address
edit LAN-Staff
set subnet 10.10.10.0/24
next
end
config firewall policy
edit 0
set name Staff-Internet
set srcintf internal
set dstintf wan1
set srcaddr LAN-Staff
set dstaddr all
set action accept
set schedule always
set service ALL
set nat enable
next
end

parts.explain:
FortiOS order for a new session: route lookup first (which also decides the egress interface), then the policy for
that interface pair, then NAT. No route means no policy match is even attempted. Using an address object instead of
'all' documents intent and keeps rogue subnets out.

parts.title: Publish the appointment portal
parts.brief:
Patients book at **https://citas.clinicasanrafael.co** (DNS already points to 203.0.113.2). Publish WEB-CITAS on
wan1's IP, HTTPS only. The portal logs client IPs for audit, so the server must see the patient's real address.
tasks: VIP VIP-CITAS-443: 203.0.113.2:443 on wan1 → 192.168.50.10:443 (port forwarding).
Policy wan1 → dmz to the VIP, service HTTPS only, no NAT.
Test from HOME-PC: curl https://citas.clinicasanrafael.co

checks.text: A patient (HOME-PC) reaches the portal over HTTPS
WEB-CITAS sees the patient's real IP (100.25.7.9)
SSH to the portal is not exposed

hints: A VIP is just the translation. Nothing passes until a policy uses the VIP as destination.
`config firewall vip` / `edit VIP-CITAS-443` / `set extip 203.0.113.2` / `set mappedip 192.168.50.10` / `set extintf wan1` / `set portforward enable` / `set extport 443` / `set mappedport 443`.
In the policy, `set dstaddr VIP-CITAS-443` and `set service HTTPS`; leave NAT disabled so the server sees real client IPs.

solution.FGT-SR:
config firewall vip
edit VIP-CITAS-443
set extip 203.0.113.2
set mappedip 192.168.50.10
set extintf wan1
set portforward enable
set extport 443
set mappedport 443
next
end
config firewall policy
edit 0
set name Citas-Publish
set srcintf wan1
set dstintf dmz
set srcaddr all
set dstaddr VIP-CITAS-443
set action accept
set schedule always
set service HTTPS
next
end

parts.explain:
With port forwarding the VIP translates only TCP 443, so 22 and 80 still go to the FortiGate itself (and are dropped,
because wan1 allows only ping). Enabling NAT on an inbound policy would hide every patient behind the DMZ interface IP
and break the portal's audit log: a classic day-two complaint.

parts.title: Hand-over hardening
parts.brief:
Before hand-over, the clinic's security officer wants admin logins limited to the staff LAN, a 10-minute idle timeout,
and the final config saved to the NAS.
tasks: Trusted host for the admin account: 10.10.10.0/24.
Admin idle timeout: 10 minutes.
Back up the configuration to TFTP 10.10.10.50.

checks.text: admin can only log in from 10.10.10.0/24

hints: Trusted hosts are per admin: `config system admin` / `edit admin` / `set trusthost1 10.10.10.0/24`.
Backup: `execute backup config tftp <file> 10.10.10.50`.

solution.FGT-SR:
config system admin
edit admin
set trusthost1 10.10.10.0/24
next
end
config system global
set admintimeout 10
end
execute backup config tftp fgt-sr-handover.conf 10.10.10.50

parts.explain:
Trusted hosts are checked on top of allowaccess: an address outside them can't log in even where HTTPS is allowed.
Configure them on every admin account, or the one you forget becomes the way in. The final backup goes into the
hand-over pack with the as-built document.

tasks: Address LAB-ANALYZERS: range 10.10.10.60-10.10.10.69. Address XRAY-01: 10.10.10.70/32.

Address VENDOR-LIS: FQDN soporte.historiaclinica.co.
Allow GRP-MEDICAL → VENDOR-LIS on HTTPS and DNS; deny GRP-MEDICAL to anything else. Mind the policy order.

checks.text: ANALYZER-01 reaches the vendor cloud on HTTPS
XRAY-01 reaches the vendor and nothing else
The vendor object is an FQDN, not a hard-coded IP

hints: The analyzers are inside 10.10.10.0/24, so policy 1 (Staff-Internet) matches them first. Your new policies must sit above it.
Ranges: `set type iprange` / `set start-ip` / `set end-ip`. FQDN: `set type fqdn` / `set fqdn soporte.historiaclinica.co`.
Create the allow and the deny with `edit 0`, then `move <id> before 1` for both, allow above deny.

config firewall address
edit LAB-ANALYZERS
set type iprange
set start-ip 10.10.10.60
set end-ip 10.10.10.69
next
edit XRAY-01
set subnet 10.10.10.70/32
next
edit VENDOR-LIS
set type fqdn
set fqdn soporte.historiaclinica.co
next
end
config firewall addrgrp
edit GRP-MEDICAL
set member LAB-ANALYZERS XRAY-01
next
end
config firewall policy
edit 10
set name Medical-to-Vendor
set srcintf internal
set dstintf wan1
set srcaddr GRP-MEDICAL
set dstaddr VENDOR-LIS
set action accept
set schedule always
set service HTTPS
set nat enable
next
edit 11
set name Medical-DNS
set srcintf internal
set dstintf wan1
set srcaddr GRP-MEDICAL
set dstaddr all
set action accept
set schedule always
set service DNS
set nat enable
next
edit 12
set name Medical-Deny
set srcintf internal
set dstintf wan1
set srcaddr GRP-MEDICAL
set dstaddr all
set action deny
set schedule always
set service ALL
next
move 10 before 1
move 11 before 1
move 12 before 1
end

parts.explain:
FortiOS evaluates policies top-down and stops at the first match. A specific rule below a broad one never fires, which
is why "I added a block and it does nothing" is one of the most common tickets. FQDN objects follow the vendor's DNS, so
a cloud provider changing IPs doesn't break the clinic. The device needs DNS too, or the FQDN connection never starts.

checks.text: RDP from CONSULTORIO is now denied by policy 4
Proved the match with a lookup or a debug

ran.fail: Show evidence first: `diagnose firewall iprope lookup <src> <sport> 52.10.20.30 3389 tcp internal`.

answer.hint: Which policy did the lookup return?
answer.why: Policy 1 accepts ALL from LAN-Staff and sits above policy 4; FortiOS stops at the first match.

move 4 before 1
end

parts.explain:

The security team noticed that when the tunnel is down, Cali's traffic to 10.20.0.0/16 follows the default route and

tasks: Each side: a blackhole route to the remote LAN with distance 254.
Prove it: answer what route Cali uses for 10.20.10.20 if the tunnel goes down.

checks.text: FGT-CLO has a blackhole for 10.20.0.0/16 at distance 254
FGT-BOG has a blackhole for 10.30.0.0/24 at distance 254
Traffic still flows while the tunnel is up
If VPN-BOG drops, which route does FGT-CLO use for 10.20.10.20?

answer.hint: A route through a down tunnel leaves the table. What's left with the next-best distance?
answer.why: The blackhole (distance 254) takes over, so the traffic is dropped instead of leaking out wan1 in clear text.

hints: Think about what's left in the routing table once the tunnel's route disappears.
`set blackhole enable` and `set distance 254` in a new static route; no device or gateway.

edit 0
set dst 10.20.0.0/16
set blackhole enable
set distance 254
next
end
solution.FGT-BOG:

edit 0
set dst 10.30.0.0/24
set blackhole enable
set distance 254
next
end

parts.explain:
When a tunnel goes down FortiOS removes the routes through it; without a blackhole the default route takes over and
sends internal traffic, and sometimes internal DNS queries, to the ISP. The blackhole costs nothing while the tunnel is up.

parts.title: The adjacency
tasks: OSPF on FGT-BOG: router ID 10.20.255.1, the transit 10.20.50.0/29 in area 0.
Advertise the HQ LAN (10.20.10.0/24) too, without sending OSPF hellos to the PCs.
Check `get router info ospf neighbor` and the routing table.
From HQ-PC: `tnc 10.20.70.10 -port 443` (the camera recorder).

checks.text: FGT-BOG and CORE-SW are Full neighbors
FGT-BOG learns the warehouse VLAN by OSPF
No OSPF hellos on the HQ LAN

config.fail: port2 sends OSPF hellos to the PCs: make it passive.

hints: `config router ospf` / `set router-id 10.20.255.1` / `config area` / `edit 0.0.0.0` / `next` / `end` / `config network` / `edit 1` / `set prefix 10.20.50.0 255.255.255.248` / `set area 0.0.0.0`.
A network statement enables OSPF on every interface whose IP falls inside it. Add 10.20.10.0/24 as a second network and make port2 passive: `set passive-interface port2`.

solution.FGT-BOG:
config router ospf
set router-id 10.20.255.1
config area
edit 0.0.0.0
next
end
config network
edit 1
set prefix 10.20.50.0 255.255.255.248
set area 0.0.0.0
next
edit 2
set prefix 10.20.10.0 255.255.255.0
set area 0.0.0.0
next
end
set passive-interface port2
end
get router info ospf neighbor

parts.explain:
The adjacency forms because both sides agree on area, subnet and mask, hello/dead timers, authentication and
area type, and their router IDs differ. Passive interfaces (the HQ LAN here, the VLANs on the switch) are
advertised but send no hellos, so no PC can become a neighbor. Without the HQ LAN in OSPF, the switch would
have no route back to 10.20.10.0/24 and the recorder's replies would die there.

parts.title: A way out for the campus
tasks: Let CORE-SW learn a default route from FGT-BOG through OSPF (FGT-BOG keeps its static default to ETB).
Policy CAMPUS → Internet with NAT; test from WH-PC with `curl https://www.google.com`.

checks.text: CORE-SW has a default route learned from OSPF

hints: `config router ospf` / `set default-information-originate enable`: the FortiGate advertises 0.0.0.0/0 as an external route because it has a default route itself (`always` advertises it even without one).
Then a normal policy port5 → port1, source CAMPUS, NAT enabled.

solution.FGT-BOG:
config router ospf
set default-information-originate enable
end
config firewall policy
edit 4
set name "Campus-Internet"
set srcintf port5
set dstintf port1
set srcaddr CAMPUS
set dstaddr all
set action accept
set schedule always
set service ALL
set nat enable
next
end

parts.explain:
`default-information-originate enable` injects 0.0.0.0/0 as an external (E2) LSA only while the FortiGate has a
default route of its own, so if the ETB route disappears the campus stops sending traffic to a dead end. The
return traffic for the HQ LAN works the same way: the switch follows its default to the FortiGate.

parts.title: Authenticate the adjacency
parts.brief:
**Security audit finding.** OSPF without authentication lets any device on the transit inject routes. The network
team has just enabled **MD5** on CORE-SW's uplink: key ID **1**, key `Andes-OSPF-26`. The campus is down until the
FortiGate matches.
tasks: See the adjacency fail (`get router info ospf neighbor`, `diagnose ip router ospf all enable`).
Configure MD5 authentication on FGT-BOG's port5 with the same key ID and key.
hints: Authentication is per interface: `config router ospf` / `config ospf-interface` / `edit CORE` / `set interface port5` / `set authentication message-digest`.
Then `config md5-keys` / `edit 1` / `set key-string Andes-OSPF-26`. Key ID and key must match the switch.

solution.FGT-BOG:
config router ospf
config ospf-interface
edit CORE
set interface port5
set authentication message-digest
config md5-keys
edit 1
set key-string Andes-OSPF-26
next
end
next
end
end

parts.explain:
With MD5 each OSPF packet carries a hash of the packet plus the key, so a device without the key can't form an
adjacency or inject routes. Both the key ID and the key must match. Roll keys out in a maintenance window, or the
adjacency drops between the first and the second side's change, as you just saw.

configuration and the switch's ports become FortiGate-controlled. Until then, the switch passes no user traffic,
which is why authorization is a deliberate step (a rogue switch plugged into FortiLink can't join by itself).

gateway, the DHCP server and the firewall for it, and every flow between VLANs crosses a policy. The `vlan`

unknown device on it is a real risk. Shut unused ports, or put them in a dead VLAN, and consider 802.1X/MAB on

their FortiGates to accept only Andes prefixes (anything inside 10.20.0.0/16 or 10.30.0.0/16, up to /24).

set le 24
next

set le 24
next
end
next

config neighbor

next

end

parts.explain:
Filtering what you accept from a provider is basic BGP hygiene: a leak or a hijack upstream shouldn't rewrite
your routing table. `le 24` means "this prefix or anything more specific, down to /24"; without ge/le a rule
matches only the exact prefix. On a production change you'd use `execute router clear bgp ip <peer> soft in`
to apply the new filter without resetting the session.

Once the heartbeat sees a matching peer, the units elect a primary and the primary pushes its configuration. With
override enabled, priority beats uptime in the election, so FGT-A takes the role back after a reboot: decide that on

role and blackhole the site.

tasks: Launch TP-2021-44228 (Log4Shell) from the Internet attacker at citas.clinicasanrafael.co first: it reaches the server.

On Citas-Publish (policy 2): UTM on, PORTAL-IPS, and SSL profile deep-inspection (the portal is HTTPS).

checks.text: Log4Shell requests to the portal are blocked

hints: `config ips sensor` / `edit PORTAL-IPS` / `config entries` / `edit 1` / `set location server` / `set severity critical high` / `set action block` / `end`.

The IPS can only match what it can read. The attack is HTTPS: with certificate inspection (or none) the sensor sees ciphertext and lets it pass. Try the attack before and after `set ssl-ssh-profile deep-inspection`.

config ips sensor
edit PORTAL-IPS
config entries
edit 1
set location server
set severity critical high
set action block
next
end
next
end
config firewall policy
edit 2
set utm-status enable
set ips-sensor PORTAL-IPS
set ssl-ssh-profile deep-inspection
next
end

parts.explain:
An IPS sensor is a filter over the signature database: here every critical or high server-side signature, blocked.
On a policy that publishes an HTTPS server, the FortiGate needs to decrypt to see the request line and headers the
signatures key on; FortiOS does that with the server's own certificate on the SSL profile ("protecting SSL server").
Without it the sensor is on the policy and still blind.

Staff can still manage the FortiGate from the LAN

No IPS sensor applies to traffic aimed at the FortiGate itself through a firewall policy: the fix for an exposed admin interface is not exposing it (allowaccess, trusted hosts, local-in policies).

solution.FGT-SR:

edit wan1

next
end

parts.explain:
CVE-2022-40684 abused the admin REST API itself. Exposure is the root cause: admin access on an Internet-facing

hints: Users type `jperez`: that's the sAMAccountName attribute, so `set cnid sAMAccountName`. With the default `cn` the search looks for cn=jperez and finds nothing.
`set type regular` binds as the service account (`set username` = its full DN, `set password`), then searches under `set dn DC=andes,DC=local`.

solution.FGT-BOG:
config user ldap
edit DC-LDAP
set server 10.20.40.10
set cnid sAMAccountName
set dn DC=andes,DC=local
set type regular
set username "CN=svc-fortigate,OU=Service Accounts,DC=andes,DC=local"
set password Sv-FGT.2026!
next
end
diagnose test authserver ldap DC-LDAP jperez Andes.Fin26

parts.explain:
AD doesn't allow anonymous searches, so `regular` binds as a service account first, searches for
`sAMAccountName=jperez` under the base DN, then binds as the user with the typed password. `simple` skips the search
and builds the DN as `cnid=user,dn`, which only works when every user sits directly in one OU and is named by that
attribute: never the case in a real AD.

parts.title: The LDAP hardening weekend
parts.brief:
**Monday, 7:40.** Over the weekend the customer applied their domain-controller hardening baseline: LDAP signing
and channel binding are now required. Finance can't log in to the ERP any more.
tasks: Reproduce with `diagnose test authserver ldap DC-LDAP jperez Andes.Fin26` (and fnbamd debug if you want the detail).
Move DC-LDAP to LDAPS with the server's identity still verified (the DC's certificate is issued to dc01.andes.local).

checks.text: The session is encrypted (LDAPS or STARTTLS)

config.fail: DC-LDAP still sends LDAP in clear text.

checks.text: The server certificate is still checked

config.fail: Turning off server-identity-check makes it work, but then any machine with a certificate can pretend to be the DC.

hints: `set secure ldaps` and `set port 636`. Then the test fails again: the FortiGate compares the certificate name with what you typed in `server`.
Use the name on the certificate: `set server dc01.andes.local` (the FortiGate resolves it), and keep `server-identity-check enable`. In production you'd also import the AD CA and set `ca-cert`.

solution.FGT-BOG:
config user ldap
edit DC-LDAP
set server dc01.andes.local
set secure ldaps
set port 636
next
end
diagnose test authserver ldap DC-LDAP jperez Andes.Fin26

parts.explain:
With signing required, a domain controller rejects simple binds over plain LDAP ("Strong(er) authentication
required"). LDAPS (636) or STARTTLS (389) fixes it. The FortiGate checks that the certificate matches the `server`
value, so point it at the DC's FQDN instead of disabling the check. Disabling `server-identity-check` is the
common shortcut, and it makes the bind vulnerable to an impostor.

parts.explain:
With RADIUS the server decides who gets in (the NPS network policy) and tells the FortiGate which group the user
belongs to through a vendor-specific attribute, Fortinet-Group-Name. The FortiGate's match entry compares that value
with `group-name`. Two classic gotchas: NPS silently drops requests from an IP that isn't a RADIUS client (you see a
timeout, not a reject), and a wrong shared secret shows up as a reject, because the server decrypts a garbage password.

which is fine because the login page is reached by IP redirect.

labs.title: Cali overlay: two IPsec tunnels under SD-WAN
labs.brief:
**SOW 2026-180, MPLS exit.** Andes cancelled the MPLS. Cali now has two Internet links, **Emcali** (wan1, fiber) and
**Movistar** (wan2), and one IPsec tunnel to HQ over each: **HQ-EMC** and **HQ-MOV** (already up, HQ side done).

Design:
- Both tunnels are SD-WAN members in a zone **overlay**; HQ (10.20.0.0/16) is reached through the zone.
- A health check **HQ-ERP** pings the ERP (10.20.10.20) through each tunnel.
- ERP traffic (HTTPS to 10.20.10.20) must use the tunnel that meets an SLA of **latency ≤ 60 ms, packet loss ≤ 2 %**,
  preferring HQ-EMC.
- Cali's Internet stays on wan1 directly (not part of this change).

answer.why: FGT-BOG had no route to 10.30.0.0/24 through port3, so the reverse path check dropped Cali's packets on arrival.

hints: On FGT-BOG: `diagnose debug flow filter addr 10.30.0.20`, `diagnose debug enable`, `diagnose debug flow trace start 10`. Then test from CLO-PC.

solution.FGT-BOG:
diagnose debug flow filter addr 10.30.0.20
diagnose debug enable
diagnose debug flow trace start 10
config router static
edit 0
set dst 10.30.0.0/24
set gateway 10.255.0.1
set device port3
next
end

parts.explain:
The reverse path check (anti-spoofing) drops a new session whose source isn't reachable through the incoming interface.
The default route points to the ISP on port1, so 10.30.0.20 "should" come from port1, not from the MPLS. Restoring the
static route fixes both directions.

parts.explain:

or pool in the WAN subnet, the FortiGate must answer ARP (arp-reply enable, the default); for a block routed by the ISP
to the FortiGate, ARP isn't involved.

tasks: Prove where the traffic dies (routing table, debug flow or ARP table).
Fix it and answer the root cause.

answer.hint: `get router info routing-table all`: where does the default route point?
answer.why: The static default route still pointed to the old gateway 200.31.20.1, which isn't on the new 200.31.30.0/29 subnet, so FortiOS kept it inactive and HQ had no default route.

hints: `get router info routing-table all` has no default route; `get router info routing-table database` shows why.
Edit static route 1 and set gateway 200.31.30.1.

solution.FGT-BOG:
get router info routing-table all
config router static
edit 1
set gateway 200.31.30.1
next
end

parts.explain:
FortiOS only installs a static route whose gateway is reachable on the route's interface. After the readdressing, the
old gateway 200.31.20.1 was off the new subnet, so the default route stayed in the database as inactive and the
routing table had no default route: traffic to the Internet was dropped for lack of a route. ISP migrations need a
checklist: interface IP, default route, VIPs, IP pools, IPsec peers and anything the remote side whitelists.

parts.title: "The warehouse lost everything after the core switch swap"
tasks: Look at the neighbor state on FGT-BOG and find out why it's stuck.
Restore routing without touching CORE-SW.
Answer the root cause.

answer.sample: The new switch uses MTU 9000 on the uplink; FortiGate port5 is 1500, so the adjacency is stuck in ExStart
answer.hint: A neighbor that exists but never reaches Full: which state, and what is compared in that state?
answer.why: OSPF compares the interface MTU in the database description exchange. 9000 vs 1500 leaves the adjacency in ExStart: hellos work (so the integrator 'sees' the neighbor) but no routes are exchanged.

hints: `get router info ospf neighbor` shows the state; `diagnose ip router ospf all enable` + `diagnose debug enable` tells you why.
Match the MTU or tell OSPF to ignore it on port5: `config ospf-interface` / `edit CORE` / `set interface port5` / `set mtu-ignore enable`. Plan the real fix (same MTU both sides) for the next window.

solution.FGT-BOG:
get router info ospf neighbor
config router ospf
config ospf-interface
edit CORE
set interface port5
set mtu-ignore enable
next
end
end

parts.explain:
ExStart/Exchange stuck is the classic MTU symptom: the neighbors see each other's hellos (so they're "neighbors"),
but the database description packets are refused. `mtu-ignore` is the quick fix; matching MTUs is the right one,
because a 9000-byte frame towards a 1500-byte port still gets dropped.

parts.title: "OSPF never comes up after the 'fast convergence' change"
tasks: Find why there's no neighbor at all.
Restore the adjacency (the switch keeps its timers).
Answer the root cause.

answer.sample: Hello/dead intervals 2/8 on the FortiGate vs 10/40 on the switch
answer.hint: What must match in every hello for two routers to even list each other?
answer.why: Hello and dead intervals are carried in each hello and must match; otherwise the hello is discarded and the neighbor never appears. Fast failover is better done with BFD than by shrinking timers on one side.

hints: `get router info ospf interface port5` shows the timers; the switch uses 10/40.
`config router ospf` / `config ospf-interface` / `edit CORE` / `set hello-interval 10` / `set dead-interval 40` (or unset both for the defaults).

solution.FGT-BOG:
get router info ospf interface port5
config router ospf
config ospf-interface
edit CORE
set hello-interval 10
set dead-interval 40
next
end
end

parts.explain:
Unlike an MTU mismatch (stuck in ExStart), a timer mismatch means the hello is dropped, so the neighbor never shows
up at all. If the customer wants sub-second failover, use BFD on both sides rather than tiny hello timers.

answer.sample: The RMA switch has a new serial: it's only discovered, not authorized, and the port VLANs are configured under the old serial
answer.hint: What identifies a managed switch on the FortiGate?

Authorize the new serial and set port1 and port2 to SCANNERS under it (the FortiLink Guide also documents `execute replace-device fortiswitch <old> <new>`, which moves the configuration for you).

config switch-controller managed-switch
edit S148FFTF26000417
set fsw-wan1-admin enable
set description FSW-WH
config ports
edit port1
set vlan SCANNERS
next
edit port2
set vlan SCANNERS
next
end
next
end

parts.explain:
Switch configuration lives on the FortiGate, keyed by serial. For an RMA, the replace-device command moves the old
serial's configuration to the new one; otherwise you authorize the new unit and rebuild the port settings, then
delete the old entry.

Fix it and check that Cali reaches the ERP.
Answer the root cause.

answer.sample: remote-as typed as 64060 instead of 64600: the OPEN is rejected (Bad Peer AS)
answer.hint: Compare the AS the FortiGate expects with the one in the carrier's OPEN.
answer.why: Each side checks the AS in the other's OPEN message against its configured remote-as. 64060 ≠ 64600, so the FortiGate sends a NOTIFICATION (Bad Peer AS) and the session falls back to Idle.

hints: `get router info bgp neighbors` on FGT-CLO shows the last error.
`config router bgp` / `config neighbor` / `edit 10.255.0.5` / `set remote-as 64600`.

solution.FGT-CLO:
get router info bgp neighbors
config router bgp
config neighbor
edit 10.255.0.5
set remote-as 64600
next
end
end

parts.explain:
A session that flips between Idle and Active with an OPEN error is almost always AS numbers or the peer's IP. Copy
ASNs from the carrier's handover document, and read them back to them on the call.

edit DC-LDAP

next

"Everyone fails at once" is never the users' passwords. With a regular bind, the service account is a single point of
failure: put it on the AD team's rotation checklist, or use a managed account process that updates the FortiGate
(or FortiManager) in the same change.

answer.hint: Which routes does FortiOS agree to put into BGP from a network statement?
answer.why: With network-import-check enabled (the default), FortiOS advertises a network statement only if that exact prefix is in the routing table. The /16 doesn't exist, so nothing goes out.

`config router bgp` / `config network` / `edit 1` / `set prefix 10.30.0.0 255.255.255.0` (or add a blackhole static /16 if you really want the summary).

get router info bgp neighbors 10.255.0.5 advertised-routes
config router bgp
config network
edit 1
set prefix 10.30.0.0 255.255.255.0
next
end
end

parts.explain:
To advertise a summary that has no matching route, create one: a blackhole static route for 10.30.0.0/16 makes the
prefix exist (and drops traffic to unused parts of the range), which is the usual way to anchor an aggregate.

parts.title: "RADIUS times out, but NPS is up and the secret is right"
tasks: Reproduce with `diagnose test authserver radius NPS pap lgomez Contr4t1sta!`.
Find out why NPS never answers and fix it on the FortiGate (the customer won't touch NPS today).
Answer the root cause.

answer.sample: source-ip 10.20.10.1 makes requests come from an IP that isn't an NPS RADIUS client, so NPS drops them silently
answer.hint: Which IP does NPS see the request coming from?
answer.why: NPS discards requests from unknown clients without answering, so the FortiGate sees a timeout. The partner forced source-ip 10.20.10.1 (the LAN IP), but the client entry is 10.20.40.1.

hints: A timeout (not a reject) from NPS usually means NPS doesn't know the client. `show user radius NPS` and look for anything that changes the source address.
`unset source-ip` (the FortiGate then uses port4, 10.20.40.1), or set it to 10.20.40.1.

solution.FGT-BOG:
diagnose test authserver radius NPS pap lgomez Contr4t1sta!
config user radius
edit NPS
unset source-ip
next
end

parts.explain:
RADIUS servers authenticate their clients by source IP plus shared secret. A request from an unknown IP is dropped
without a reply, which looks exactly like a firewall or a dead server. Check the IP the server sees: the egress
interface by default, or `source-ip` / `nas-ip` when someone set them.

the user's group one the agent monitors and the fsso-service group contains?". Reinstalling an agent resets its
password and its monitored groups, so put both in the DC rebuild runbook.

answer.hint: What's the next hop of SALUD's default route, and is it on SALUD's link subnet?
answer.why: The cloned route kept Naviera's gateway, 10.255.1.1, which isn't on vlSAL1's subnet (10.255.2.0/30). The route can't resolve, so SALUD has no usable default route.

hints: `config vdom` / `edit SALUD` / `get router info routing-table all`: the default route is missing from the active table. Why? Look at `show router static`.

edit SALUD
show router static
config router static
edit 1
set gateway 10.255.2.1
next
end
end

parts.explain:

tasks: Reproduce from GUEST-PHONE: curl https://www.google.com.

answer.why: Deep inspection re-signs sites with the FortiGate CA; domain PCs trust it (pushed by GPO), guest phones don't.

hints: Under deep inspection the FortiGate presents its own certificate for every site.

parts.title: Get the FortiGate in
tasks: Send FGT-BOG's logs to FSIEM-01 by syslog (UDP 514).
Check the CMDB on FSIEM-01: both FGT-BOG-HQ and DC01 should be there.
hints: `config log syslogd setting` / `set status enable` / `set server 10.20.40.50`.
Syslog is local-out traffic from the FortiGate: it needs a route to 10.20.40.50 (it has one: port4 is connected), not a policy.

solution.FGT-BOG:
config log syslogd setting
set status enable
set server 10.20.40.50
end

parts.explain:
FortiSIEM learns devices from what they send: a FortiGate that starts sending syslog appears in the CMDB with its
type parsed from the log format. Windows hosts come in through the agent (or WMI/WinRM pulling), which is how
DC01 was already there.

parts.title: The morning's incidents
parts.brief: **09:15.** FortiSIEM shows new incidents. Triage them.
tasks: List the incidents and open the high-severity one.
Use analytics to build the timeline (e.g. `analytics srcIpAddr=10.20.10.66`).
Assign the high-severity incident to yourself and answer the questions.

answer.sample: jperez
answer.hint: The 4624 after the failures names the user.
answer.why: Twelve failed logons for jperez from 10.20.10.66, then a success at 08:43:41.

answer.sample: 10.20.10.66 (LT-CONTRATISTA)
answer.hint: srcIpAddr and hostName in the events.
answer.why: The contractor laptop LT-CONTRATISTA on the HQ LAN.

checks.text: What did the attacker do four minutes later, and why does it matter?

answer.sample: Installed the PSEXESVC service (event 7045): remote execution with PsExec, a sign of lateral movement
answer.hint: Search all events from that source after the success.
answer.why: PSEXESVC is the service PsExec installs to run commands remotely. Its rule is disabled by default, so only the analytics search shows it.

hints: `incidents`, then `incident <id>` for the HIGH one. `incident <id> assign <your name>`.
`analytics srcIpAddr=10.20.10.66` shows every event from the laptop, in order.

solution.FSIEM-01:
incidents
incident 7231 assign jose
analytics srcIpAddr=10.20.10.66

parts.explain:
A burst of failures followed by a success is the classic password-guessing pattern; the correlation rule turns
13 events into one high-severity incident. The service installation right after shows why triage doesn't stop
at the incident: the timeline from analytics tells you what the attacker did next.

parts.title: Tune out the nightly scanner
parts.brief:
**SOC review.** Every night the vulnerability scanner (NESSUS-SCAN, 10.20.40.30) trips "Excessive Windows Logon
Failures" against DC01. It's authorized, scheduled and noisy. Andes asks you to stop the noise without blinding
the rule.
tasks: Add an exception for the scanner's source IP to that rule. Don't disable the rule.

checks.text: No more failures incident for the scanner
The contractor laptop is still detected

hints: `rules`, then `rule "Excessive Windows Logon Failures" exception srcIpAddr=10.20.40.30`.
Disabling the rule would also hide the real attack you just triaged.

solution.FSIEM-01:
rule "Excessive Windows Logon Failures" exception srcIpAddr=10.20.40.30
incidents

parts.explain:
Tuning means narrowing, not silencing: an exception for one known source keeps the rule working for everything
else. Document every exception (who asked, why, review date): unreviewed exceptions are how attackers hide in
plain sight.

parts.explain:
EDR collectors register with the aggregator on TCP 8081 and send events to the core on TCP 555; a missing firewall rule leaves endpoints unprotected
without anyone noticing, because the endpoint looks fine. Check the inventory on day one and alert on
disconnected collectors.

parts.title: Triage the alert
parts.brief:
**10:14.** FEDR-01 raised a Malicious event on FIN-PC (Juan Pérez, Finance). Policies are still in simulation,
so nothing was blocked.
tasks: Read the event and its flow analyzer view.
Contain: kill the process and delete the file, and isolate FIN-PC.
Answer the questions.

checks.text: Isolated FIN-PC can't reach the Internet

answer.sample: From an email attachment: OUTLOOK.EXE started Factura_Nov.pdf.exe
answer.hint: Look at the parent in forensics.
answer.why: The flow analyzer shows OUTLOOK.EXE → Factura_Nov.pdf.exe: a double-extension attachment opened from email.

checks.text: Which external IP should the FortiGate block?

answer.hint: Destinations in the event details.
answer.why: The payload connected to 185.220.101.47:443, its command-and-control server.

hints: `events`, then `event <id>` and `forensics <id>`.
`remediate <id> kill`, `remediate <id> delete`, then `isolate FIN-PC`.

solution.FEDR-01:
events
forensics 1001
remediate 1001 kill
remediate 1001 delete
isolate FIN-PC

parts.explain:
Isolation keeps the host talking only to the EDR manager, so you can still investigate and remediate while it
can't spread or reach its C2. The flow analyzer answers the two questions every incident report needs: how it
got in, and where it talked to.

parts.title: Switch to prevention
tasks: Put Ransomware Prevention and Execution Prevention in prevention mode.
Block 185.220.101.47 on FGT-BOG for all outbound traffic (address + a deny policy above the Internet policy).

checks.text: Ransomware Prevention is in prevention mode
Execution Prevention is in prevention mode
HQ can't reach the C2 any more

hints: `policy "Ransomware Prevention" prevention`, same for Execution Prevention.
Address C2-185.220.101.47, a deny policy port2 → port1 to it, moved above policy 1 (`move 6 before 1`).

solution.FEDR-01:
policy "Ransomware Prevention" prevention

Registration (8081) and event delivery (555) are different paths. A collector can show as connected while its
events never arrive, so the inventory alone isn't proof: check that events from a test endpoint reach the manager.

parts.title: Stop a miner
tasks: Put Execution Prevention in Prevention mode on FEDR-01.
Run the endpoint test Miner (CPU) on FIN-PC and wait for the event (about 90 seconds on the real network).

checks.text: Execution Prevention is in Prevention mode
The miner raised Suspicious Resource Usage on FIN-PC and was blocked

hints: Console > Security Settings, or `policy "Execution Prevention" prevention`.
The rule needs the CPU near the host's cap for 90 s: the collector reports every 2 s from the host's cgroup.
parts.explain:
In Prevention mode the manager kills the process on the host (on the real network you can watch it disappear from
the Linux shell's `ps`). Behaviour rules catch what signatures can't: a miner is often a legitimate binary.

tasks: Look at the event, decide whether it's a false positive, and fix it without weakening the policy.
Answer the root cause.

checks.text: An exception covers the updater for that rule
Execution Prevention stays in prevention mode

answer.sample: A signed vendor updater running from a Temp folder triggers the Unconfirmed Executable rule: a false positive
answer.hint: Who signed it, where does it run from, and which rule fired?
answer.why: The updater is signed by the ERP vendor and launched by their service, but it runs from a Temp path that the rule treats as suspicious. An exception for that process and rule fixes it; simulation mode would remove protection for everything.

parts.explain:

one false positive leaves every endpoint unprotected against everything that policy covers.

checks.text: An incident exists from your handler
Which source, and how many attempts?

answer.sample: 103.145.13.21, 14 attempts with common usernames
answer.hint: The handler's event shows the source and count.
answer.why: 14 failures from 103.145.13.21 trying admin, test, root… a password-spraying pattern.

hints: `logview event subtype=vpn` shows the field values (action=ssl-login-fail).
`handler create "SSL-VPN brute force" type=event subtype=vpn action=ssl-login-fail threshold=10`, then `alerts` and `incident create <id>`.

alerts
incident create 101 assign=jose

parts.explain:
Thresholds turn noise into signal: one failed login is a typo, 14 from one IP with dictionary usernames is
spraying. Next steps for the customer: MFA on the VPN, geo or reputation blocking for the portal, and a lockout
policy.

parts.title: 23:40 — triage
tasks: List FSIEM-01's incidents. Take ownership of the logon-failures incident for 10.20.10.66.
With analytics, find out whether any of the attempted accounts logged on successfully afterwards.
Check FEDR-01's events too: is there anything on the FortiEDR side tonight?

checks.text: The failures incident for the contractor laptop is assigned
Which account did the spraying get?

answer.sample: svc_sqlrpt
answer.hint: Look for a 4624 from 10.20.10.66 after the burst of 4625.
answer.why: Fourteen different accounts failed once each, then svc_sqlrpt logged on at 23:14:21: spraying, and a service account with a guessable password.

checks.text: Why didn't 'Successful Logon After Multiple Failures' fire?

answer.sample: That rule needs many failures for the same user; spraying tries each account once, so no user reaches the threshold
answer.hint: Read the rule's description: what does it group by?
answer.why: The built-in rule correlates failures and a success for the same user and source. A spray spreads one attempt per account, so it never crosses the per-user threshold. That's a detection gap you'll close in part b.

checks.text: What else is happening tonight, and on which machine?

answer.sample: FIN-PC (CFO jperez) ran a fake invoice that started rundll32 talking to 185.220.101.47 — a separate phishing infection
answer.hint: `events` on FEDR-01, and `analytics destIpAddr=185.220.101.47` on FSIEM-01.
answer.why: Two incidents: an AD attack from the contractor laptop and a phishing infection on the CFO's PC beaconing to a known malicious address. They aren't linked by any evidence so far; treat them as separate until proven otherwise.

hints: `incidents`, `incident <id> assign <name>`, then `analytics srcIpAddr=10.20.10.66`.
On FEDR-01: `events`, then `forensics <id>` for the process tree.

solution.FSIEM-01:
incidents
incident 7165 assign jose
analytics srcIpAddr=10.20.10.66

parts.explain:
Triage is about separating signals. The spray and the CFO's infection share a night, not a cause. Naming the
gap in the built-in rule (it groups by user) is as useful to the customer as the incident itself.

parts.title: The rules that weren't there
parts.brief:
**00:05.** The analytics show more from svc_sqlrpt after 23:14, but FortiSIEM raised nothing for it. Before you go
further, write the two detections the night needs, so the SOC sees it next time. The rules' names must match
exactly; each is replayed against tonight's attack and a normal week.
tasks: Write a rule named `Kerberoasting - RC4 TGS burst`: 4769 with RC4 (0x17), grouped by account and source, 10 or more distinct service names in 5 minutes.
Write a rule named `DCSync from non-DC account`: 4662 whose properties contain the replication rights GUID 1131f6aa, by an account that isn't a computer account (doesn't end in $).
Run `incidents` again: what does the DCSync incident tell you about the attacker's reach?

checks.text: Kerberoasting rule fires on the attack and stays quiet on a normal week
DCSync rule fires on the attack and ignores DC-to-DC replication
What does DCSync by svc_backup mean for Andes?

answer.sample: svc_backup could replicate every account's secrets, including krbtgt: assume the whole domain's credentials are compromised
answer.hint: What does a replication request return?
answer.why: DCSync asks a DC for password data the way another DC would. With Get-Changes-All the attacker can pull every hash, including krbtgt, which means forged tickets. This is now a domain compromise, not one stolen account.

hints: `rule new "Kerberoasting - RC4 TGS burst" where eventType=Win-Security-4769 ticketEncType=0x17 group user,srcIpAddr distinct svcName >= 10 window 300 sev 9`
Properties hold the GUIDs: `properties=~1131f6aa`, and the account filter `user=!*$` excludes computer accounts such as DC02$.

solution.FSIEM-01:
rule new "Kerberoasting - RC4 TGS burst" where eventType=Win-Security-4769 ticketEncType=0x17 group user,srcIpAddr distinct svcName >= 10 window 300 sev 9
rule new "DCSync from non-DC account" where eventType=Win-Security-4662 properties=~1131f6aa user=!*$ group user,srcIpAddr count >= 1 window 60 sev 10
incidents

parts.explain:
Both rules count what the technique must do. Kerberoasting needs many service tickets, so distinct service names
per requester separates it from the legacy app that asks for two services with RC4 all day. DCSync needs the
replication rights, and only DCs should use them: excluding computer accounts removes normal replication without
hiding a user or service account that was granted the rights.

parts.title: Contain — and the CISO calls
parts.brief:
**00:20.** You propose isolating FIN-PC and the contractor laptop. The CISO calls: *"The CFO is presenting to the
board from FIN-PC at 07:00 and the deck is on that laptop. Do not cut her off. Stop the bad stuff, keep the
laptop working."* The contractor laptop has no EDR.
tasks: Contain LT-CONTRATISTA (10.20.10.66) on FGT-BOG: it must not reach DC-01 any more. HQ-PC must keep reaching it.
Do NOT isolate FIN-PC. Instead stop its traffic to 185.220.101.47 on FGT-BOG, and make sure it still reaches DC-01.
Tell the customer which two accounts must be reset first.

checks.text: FIN-PC can't reach the C2 address any more
FIN-PC still reaches DC-01 (the CFO keeps working)
Which two accounts get reset first?

answer.sample: svc_sqlrpt and svc_backup
answer.hint: One was sprayed, one was used for DCSync.
answer.why: svc_sqlrpt was guessed and used for Kerberoasting; svc_backup (likely cracked from its ticket) ran DCSync. Then privileged accounts and krbtgt twice, as planned in M13.03.

hints: Two addresses (10.20.10.66/32 and 185.220.101.47/32), two deny policies on FGT-BOG, and `move` them above policies 1 and 2.
Isolation would cut the CFO off; a deny policy for one destination keeps everything else working.

solution.FGT-BOG:

set subnet 10.20.10.66 255.255.255.255
next

set action deny
set schedule always

set logtraffic all
next
edit 11

set srcintf port2
set dstintf port1
set srcaddr HQ-LAN
set dstaddr C2-185.220.101.47

set schedule always

move 11 before 1
end

parts.explain:
The requirement changed mid-incident, as it does in real life: the business decided the CFO's laptop stays up.
Network-level containment at the FortiGate stops the known C2 path without cutting her off, and an unmanaged
laptop can only be contained on the network anyway. On FortiTatake OS these checks are decided by the kernel:
the deny policies become nftables rules and the probes are real packets.

parts.title: 00:40 — the SIEM went quiet

cli.lines:
config log syslogd setting
set server 10.20.40.150
end

parts.brief:
**00:40.** A night operator "cleaned up" FGT-BOG's logging settings at 00:31. Since then FSIEM-01 shows no new
FortiGate events — in the middle of an incident. The operator swears nothing changed.
tasks: Find why FGT-BOG's syslog stopped reaching FSIEM-01 and fix it.
Confirm with a sniffer that syslog packets go to 10.20.40.50 again.

answer.sample: The syslog server was changed to 10.20.40.150 instead of FSIEM-01's 10.20.40.50
answer.hint: `show log syslogd setting` on FGT-BOG.
answer.why: One mistyped address silently blinds the SOC. That's why log-source health alerts (a source going quiet) belong in every SOC design.

hints: `show log syslogd setting` and `diagnose sniffer packet any 'udp port 514' 4 5`.

solution.FGT-BOG:
config log syslogd setting
set server 10.20.40.50
end

parts.explain:
Mid-incident faults happen. The fix is one line; the lesson is a detection for a source going quiet, so the next
time it's a P2 alert instead of a lucky glance at a dashboard.

parts.title: 02:00 — the customer update
parts.brief:
**02:00.** The CISO wants a written update before she sleeps: what happened, what you did, what's still open,
what she must decide.
tasks: Answer the four questions as you'd write them to the CISO.

checks.text: How did the attacker get in?

answer.sample: Password spraying from the unmanaged contractor laptop guessed svc_sqlrpt's password
answer.hint: Part a.
answer.why: Initial access was a guessable service-account password tried from a device the SOC couldn't see on the endpoint.

checks.text: What is contained, and what isn't yet?

answer.sample: The contractor laptop is blocked and FIN-PC can't reach the C2; the stolen credentials and possible forged tickets are not contained until the resets are done
answer.hint: Network vs credentials.
answer.why: Network containment is done; credential containment (resets, krbtgt twice) is the open item, because DCSync exposed every hash.

answer.sample: Approve the krbtgt double reset and the privileged/service account resets, which will log some services out
answer.hint: What has business impact and needs her authority?
answer.why: A domain-wide credential reset disrupts services; it's her call, with your plan and timing.

hints: Executives need impact, actions, open items and decisions — not event IDs.
Separate the two threads: AD compromise and the CFO's phishing infection.
parts.explain:
The update closes the loop: what's contained, what isn't, and the decision only the customer can make. The
technical work is wasted if the executive can't act on it at 02:00.

labs.title: Capstone · Detection sprint: four techniques, four rules, zero noise
labs.brief:
**Capstone · purple-team follow-up.** Last month's pentest at Andes reached Domain Admin and FortiSIEM stayed
silent. The pentesters left their replay files; Andes left a normal week of logs. For each technique you write one
FortiSIEM rule on **FSIEM-01**: it must fire on the replay and stay quiet on the normal week. The checks replay
both streams through your rule.

Rule syntax (type `help` on FSIEM-01):
`rule new "<name>" where key=value ... group a,b count|distinct <attr> >= N window <seconds> [sev N]`.
Values take `*` globs, `a|b` alternatives, `~text` (contains) and a leading `!` (not). Use `analytics` to look at the
fields: `user`, `srcIpAddr`, `svcName`, `ticketEncType`, `logonType`, `logonProcess`, `properties`, `shareName`,
`preAuthType`, `failureCode`, `targetImage`, `grantedAccess`, `procName`, `parentProcName`.

parts.title: Spraying over Kerberos
parts.brief:
The pentesters sprayed over Kerberos, not NTLM: the DC logs **4771** (pre-authentication failed) with failure
code **0x18** (bad password). The normal week has users who mistype their password a few times.
tasks: Write `Kerberos password spray`: 4771 with failure code 0x18, grouped by source address, 8 or more distinct users in 30 minutes.

checks.text: Kerberos password spray: fires on the replay, quiet on the normal week

hints: Group by `srcIpAddr` and count `distinct user`: spraying is breadth, mistyping is depth.
The 0x12 failures in the baseline are disabled/expired accounts touched by a script, not bad passwords: filter `failureCode=0x18`.

solution.FSIEM-01: rule new "Kerberos password spray" where eventType=Win-Security-4771 failureCode=0x18 group srcIpAddr distinct user >= 8 window 1800 sev 8

parts.explain:
Per-user rules miss sprays by design. Counting distinct users per source catches the breadth, and the failure
code keeps unrelated failures (disabled accounts, clock skew) out.

parts.title: AS-REP roasting
parts.brief:
One account, **svc_scan**, doesn't require Kerberos pre-authentication. The pentesters asked for its TGT and
cracked it offline. Normal TGT requests use pre-authentication type 2; the roast shows **type 0**.
tasks: Write `AS-REP roast`: 4768 with pre-authentication type 0.
Tell Andes the preventive fix in one line (answer below).

checks.text: AS-REP roast: fires on the replay, quiet on the normal week
What prevents AS-REP roasting of svc_scan?

answer.sample: Turn pre-authentication back on for svc_scan (untick 'Do not require Kerberos preauthentication') and give it a long random password
answer.hint: What setting made the account roastable?
answer.why: Without pre-authentication anyone can request a TGT encrypted with the account's key. Requiring it closes the hole; a long random password makes any captured hash useless.

hints: `where eventType=Win-Security-4768 preAuthType=0 ... count >= 1 window 60`.
svc_scan also appears in the baseline with type 2: filter on the type, not the account.

solution.FSIEM-01: rule new "AS-REP roast" where eventType=Win-Security-4768 preAuthType=0 group user,srcIpAddr count >= 1 window 60 sev 8

parts.explain:
Filtering on the account name would miss the next roastable account and fire on svc_scan's normal logons.
Pre-authentication type 0 is the technique's fingerprint.

parts.title: PsExec-style lateral movement
parts.brief:
With a cracked admin password the pentesters moved to FS01 the classic way: a network logon, access to ADMIN$,
then a new service. Andes' IT runs a deployment tool that also touches ADMIN$ every morning, but never installs
services.
tasks: Write `Remote service install via ADMIN$`: on the file server, 7045 service installs whose service name is PSEXESVC or a random-looking name the pentest used (see the replay); keep it to 7045 so the deployment tool's ADMIN$ access doesn't fire.

checks.text: Remote service install: fires on the replay, quiet on the normal week

hints: `where eventType=Win-Security-7045 svcName=PSEXESVC|xQzLmP`, grouped by host (`reptDevName`).
The baseline has legitimate services installed by SYSTEM: filter on the user too (`user=!SYSTEM`) for a sturdier rule.

solution.FSIEM-01: rule new "Remote service install via ADMIN$" where eventType=Win-Security-7045 user=!SYSTEM group reptDevName,user count >= 1 window 600 sev 8

parts.explain:
The deployment tool touches ADMIN$ but never installs services; legitimate installs come from SYSTEM during
patching. A service installed by a named admin account over the network is rare and worth a human look. Matching
only PSEXESVC would miss renamed tools like the one at 10:09.

parts.title: LSASS memory read
parts.brief:
The last technique: dumping LSASS on a workstation. Sysmon event **10** (process access) shows the target image
and the access mask. Andes' antivirus and the EDR read LSASS legitimately all day.
tasks: Write `LSASS access by unusual process`: Sysmon 10 with target lsass.exe, excluding the two security products' processes you'll find in the baseline.

checks.text: LSASS access: fires on the replay, quiet on the normal week

hints: `where eventType=Win-Sysmon-10 targetImage=*lsass.exe procName=!*FortiEDRCollectorService.exe|*MsMpEng.exe`
Excluding by full image path is safer than excluding anything under Program Files: attackers can drop tools there too.

solution.FSIEM-01: rule new "LSASS access by unusual process" where eventType=Win-Sysmon-10 targetImage=*lsass.exe procName=!*FortiEDRCollectorService.exe|*MsMpEng.exe group reptDevName,procName count >= 1 window 60 sev 9

parts.explain:
Credential dumping needs one read of LSASS, so thresholds don't help; precision comes from excluding the known
readers by exact image. The rundll32 line is the comsvcs.dll MiniDump trick: a signed Windows binary, which is
why excluding 'signed' or 'System32' would have hidden it.
